+# Framing: Can molecular mapping of AAV capsid–receptor interactions on brain microvascular endothelial cells determine transcytosis vs. intracellular fate?
+
+## 1. What the question is actually asking (operational definitions)
+
+Before answering, I will define the terms so the question has a sharp, testable meaning.
+
+- **Molecular mapping** = for each AAV capsid variant, enumerating its interactions with the surface of brain microvascular endothelial cells (BMECs): (a) receptor / attachment-factor **identity** (AAVR/KIAA0319L, transferrin receptor TfR1, LY6A/LY6C1, CA4, ALPL, terminal galactose, heparan sulfate proteoglycan/HSPG, integrins, etc.); (b) binding **affinity** (KD) and on/off kinetics; (c) **avidity/valency** (a 60-fold symmetric capsid can engage many receptor copies at once, producing apparent affinities far below the monovalent KD); (d) **epitope** (which receptor domain or loop the capsid contacts — e.g., the TfR1 apical domain vs. the transferrin-binding site); and (e) **pH-dependence** of binding (release in acidified endosomes).
+- **Transcytose** = apical (luminal) → basolateral (abluminal) transport across the BMEC with release into the brain parenchyma, *without* the capsid being retained in — or transducing — the endothelial cell itself.
+- **Remain intracellular** = the capsid is retained in the BMEC, either (i) transducing the endothelial cell (nuclear delivery, as AAV2 does) or (ii) being trapped/degraded in endolysosomal compartments and never released abluminally.
+
+So the question has two parts: (1) can the binding signature *determine* which of these two fates a given variant takes, and (2) can it specify *which* binding signatures map to each fate (i.e., a signature→fate classifier).
+
+## 2. Current understanding (relaying what is already established)
+
+**The BBB as the relevant substrate.** The blood–brain barrier is formed by BMECs joined by tight junctions with suppressed paracellular and vesicular transport, so any macromolecule that reaches the brain must use an active transcellular route, principally receptor-mediated transcytosis (RMT) or a related vesicular program (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00018-018-2982-x). RMT is a four-step process — receptor binding, endocytosis, intracellular sorting/trafficking, and abluminal exocytosis — and the fate decision (transcytosis vs. lysosomal degradation vs. retention) is made at the *sorting* step, not at the *binding* step (https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-pharmtox-010814-124852).
+
+**AAV capsid architecture and the site of receptor binding.** AAV is a ~25 nm, T=1 icosahedral particle built from 60 copies of VP1/VP2/VP3 in roughly a 1:1:10 ratio (https://www.mdpi.com/1999-4915/13/1/101). The common VP3 core is an eight-stranded β-barrel whose inter-strand loops form nine variable regions (VR-I…VR-IX) that constitute the surface topology and the receptor/antibody footprints (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9479082/). Receptor-binding residues cluster at the three-fold protrusions and the 2/5-fold wall (https://www.pnas.org/doi/full/10.1073/pnas.162250899; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6537878/). Because a capsid presents 60 copies of its surface, receptor engagement is inherently **multivalent/avid**, and engineered variants typically differ only in a short peptide (e.g., a 7-mer inserted after VP1 residue 588 in AAV9) (https://www.nature.com/articles/nbt.3440).
+
+**The two canonical fates, side by side, in the same cell type.** In primary human BMEC cultures, AAV2 and AAV9 partition oppositely: AAV2 transduces BMECs and remains intracellular with perinuclear/nuclear accumulation, while AAV9 is transported across the monolayer. AAV9's crossing is active (89.7% reduction at 4 °C) whereas AAV2's is temperature-independent/paracellular-leak associated (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5298820/; https://doi.org/10.1111/jnc.13861). So the same cell type exhibits both fates depending on the capsid.
+
+**The receptor identity encodes a trafficking program.** The variants that robustly cross the BBB bind receptors whose endogenous trafficking is transcytotic or raft-associated:
+- AAV9 was the first serotype shown to cross the BBB after intravenous delivery in mice, transducing CNS neurons/astrocytes (https://www.nature.com/articles/nbt.1515).
+- AAV-PHP.B and AAV-PHP.eB, selected by Cre-recombination-based targeted evolution (CREATE), cross the BBB ~40-fold (or more) better than AAV9 in C57BL/6J mice (https://www.nature.com/articles/nbt.3440), and this phenotype was mapped, by whole-exome linkage and knockout/blocking experiments, to direct binding of the capsid to the GPI-anchored protein **LY6A (Sca-1)** with sub-nanomolar *apparent* (avid) affinity (0.07 nM), whereas the non-crossing parent AAV9 does not detectably bind LY6A (https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/molecular-therapy/fulltext/S1525-0016(19)30054-1).
+- LY6A is a mouse-specific gene: primates lack a homolog, which explains why AAV-PHP.B fails to cross in non-human primates and instead showed dose-limiting acute toxicity (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5911151/).
+- BI-hTFR1 was engineered to bind the **apical domain of human transferrin receptor (TfR1)**, a canonical RMT receptor at the BBB; it is actively transported across human brain endothelial monolayers and gives 40–50× more CNS expression than AAV9 in human-TFRC knock-in mice, with no enhancement in wild-type mice (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adm8386; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10769326/). TfR1 transcytoses iron-bound transferrin across brain capillary endothelium without lysosomal degradation (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8967351/).
+- VCAP-102 crosses via the GPI-anchored protein **ALPL** (tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase), with >100-fold transcytosis upon ectopic ALPL expression (https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/molecular-therapy/fulltext/S1525-0016(25)00373-9). Several other BBB-crossing capsids (PHP.B → LY6A, BI28 → LY6C1, AAV-F → Car4) all bind GPI-anchored proteins (https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adm8386).
+
+**A universal receptor that does not, by itself, decide fate.** AAVR (KIAA0319L) is a type-I transmembrane protein that is essential for infection by all tested AAV serotypes and binds AAV2 with ~150 nM affinity; AAVR traffics to the trans-Golgi network (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature16465; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4962915/). Critically, both transcytosing (AAV9) and non-transcytosing (AAV2) capsids use AAVR — so AAVR binding alone cannot distinguish fates; the discriminating information lives in the *additional* attachment factors and their trafficking programs.
+
+## 3. The mechanistic crux: binding is upstream of — and not identical to — the fate decision
+
+Three observations show that the fate decision is **not** a pure function of "which receptor is bound":
+
+1. **Binding identity alone does not determine outcome.** BR1 (an AAV2-derived variant) transduces BMECs with little transcytosis, yet a single Q→N substitution at position 587 (BR1N) confers strong BBB penetration while using the *same* receptor. The authors state this directly: "receptor binding alone does not determine the final outcome in vivo" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10036519/).
+2. **Valency/affinity flips the sorting decision on the same receptor.** For TfR1, bivalent or high-affinity engagement drives the antibody–receptor complex to lysosomes, while monovalent or lower-affinity engagement is sorted into transcytosis; receptor clustering that blocks entry into sorting tubules is the proposed mechanism (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00018-018-2982-x). This is exactly why a binding *signature* must include valency/affinity/epitope/pH-dependence, not just identity.
+3. **Transcytosis and transduction can be anti-correlated on the same receptor.** Blocking AAV transcytosis (e.g., with tannic acid) *increases* transduction of barrier epithelia, indicating that the fraction of capsids that would have transcytosed instead becomes available for intracellular infection — i.e., transcytosis is partly a default that competes with intracellular retention (https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/molecular-therapy/fulltext/S1525-0016(05)01698-9).
+
+## 4. Predictions
+
+**P1 (fate is underdetermined by receptor identity alone).** Any mapping that reports only *which* receptors a capsid binds will fail to separate transcytosing from intracellular variants, because both AAV2 and AAV9 engage AAVR, and BR1/BR1N share a receptor yet take opposite fates. I predict a classifier using receptor identity alone achieves ~chance separation on the known variant set.
+
+**P2 (an extended binding signature is largely — but not perfectly — sufficient).** If "molecular mapping" is extended to the composite signature {receptor identity, avidity/valency, affinity, epitope, pH-dependence}, the known variants separate cleanly: transcytosing variants engage GPI-anchored proteins (LY6A, LY6C1, Car4, ALPL) or an RMT receptor at a non-ligand-competitive epitope with moderate avidity (BI-hTFR1 on the TfR1 apical domain), while intracellular variants engage HSPG/AAVR-dominated routes with high-avidity or lysosome-routing engagement. I predict a learned classifier on this composite signature generalizes to held-out *known* variants but **fails out-of-domain** (new receptors, new species) because the mapping signature→fate is not derivable from binding physics alone.
+
+**P3 (a single-residue flip cannot be predicted from static binding maps).** The BR1N Q587N result, and the TfR1 valency switch, imply that fate is set by downstream sorting (receptor clustering, tubule entry, GPI-anchored-protein-enriched/GEEC routing), which is not encoded in a static capsid–receptor interaction map. I predict docking/MD of the capsid–receptor interface alone will *not* recapitulate these flips without trafficking data.
+
+**P4 (the literal answer is "partially yes, with a specific signature definition").** Molecular mapping can determine transcytosis vs. intracellular fate only if (i) the signature includes the *identity of the primary attachment factor/receptor* (because identity is a proxy for the trafficking program), plus (ii) quantitative valency/affinity/epitope features (because the same receptor can route either way), and (iii) the mapping is calibrated per-species (because LY6A does not exist in primates). It cannot determine fate from binding in the absence of receptor-trafficking knowledge, because binding is necessary but not sufficient.
+
+## 5. Is this compute-bound?
+
+**The determining step is empirical, not computational.** The causal link "binding signature → transcytosis vs. intracellular" is established by *measured* trafficking outcomes (transwell transport, in vivo biodistribution, sorting assays), not by solving equations. The decisive counterexamples — BR1N's single-residue flip, the TfR1 valency/affinity switch, AAV2 vs. AAV9 on the same universal receptor — are observations that no amount of docking compute would have produced a priori, because the fate decision is executed by the endothelial cell's sorting machinery (clustering, tubule entry, GEEC/caveolae routing, abluminal exocytosis), which is not a function of the binding interface.
+
+**Where compute *does* help — and why it is not the binding constraint:**
+1. *Scaling the mapping itself.* High-throughput structural prediction/docking (AlphaFold-style or Rosetta) of many variants against candidate BMEC receptors (AAVR, TfR1, LY6A/LY6C1, Car4, ALPL, galactose, HSPG) could enumerate binding signatures for thousands of sequences. This expands the (sequence→binding) map, but the map's downstream half (binding→fate) still requires experimental labels.
+2. *Simulating sorting.* Molecular dynamics of capsid–receptor valency/clustering and endosomal sorting is far from able to predict tubule entry or GEEC routing at the fidelity and timescale needed; it is a research program, not a reliable determiner.
+3. *Interpolative ML.* A model trained on (sequence + binding features → fate) could interpolate across variant space, but the label set is small (dozens of well-characterized variants), so the bottleneck is ground-truth fate data, not FLOPs.
+
+**Conclusion.** The answer to the posed question is gated by biological data and mechanism (receptor-trafficking coupling, species/strain context, endothelial sorting), not by parallel computation. More compute would refine the *binding map* but would not change the *determination* of transcytosis vs. intracellular fate, which is an empirical property of the endothelial sorting program. The problem is data- and experiment-bound, not compute-bound.
+
+VERDICT: NOT COMPUTE-BOUND

## Abstract
Delivery of genes to the brain and spinal cord across the blood-brain barrier (BBB) has not yet been achieved. Here we show that adeno-associated virus (AAV) 9 injected intravenously bypasses the BBB and efficiently targets cells of the central nervous system (CNS). Injection of AAV9-GFP into neonatal mice through the facial vein results in extensive transduction of dorsal root ganglia and motor neurons throughout the spinal cord and widespread transduction of neurons throughout the brain, including the neocortex, hippocampus and cerebellum. ## Abstract

Efficient delivery of gene therapy vectors across the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is the holy grail of neurological disease therapies. A variant of the neurotropic vector adeno-associated virus (AAV) serotype 9, called AAV-PHP.B, was shown to very efficiently deliver transgenes across the BBB in C57BL/6J mice. Based on our recent observation that this phenotype is mouse strain dependent, we used whole-exome sequencing-based genetics to map this phenotype to a specific haplotype of lymphocyte antigen 6 complex, locus A (Ly6a) (stem cell antigen-1 [Sca-1]), which encodes a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored protein whose function had been thought to be limited to the biology of hematopoiesis. Additional biochemical and genetic studies definitively linked high BBB transport to the binding of AAV-PHP.B with LY6A (SCA-1). These studies identify, for the first time, a ligand for this GPI-anchored protein and suggest a role for it in BBB transport that could be hijacked by viruses in natural infections or by gene therapy vectors to treat neurological diseases.

AAV2, the most commonly studied AAV serotype, attaches to cells using heparan sulphate proteoglycan (HSPG)5. For several other non-enveloped viruses, initial attachment is followed by engagement of a protein receptor, which dictates entry into the cytoplasm. Whether AAV also requires such a protein receptor is unclear. Surface proteins including human fibroblast growth factor receptor-1 (FGFR1) and hepatocyte growth factor receptor (c-MET) have been reported as putative AAV2 co-receptors6,7. Using isogenic knockout cell lines (Extended Data Fig. 1a, b) however, we observed no significant effect on AAV2 infection in cells lacking FGFR1, and only a minimal consequence of c-MET loss (Extended Data Fig. 1c), suggesting a modest role in AAV2 infection for these proteins. To identify host factors critical for AAV2 infection, we used an unbiased, genome-wide screening approach based on insertional mutagenesis in haploid human cells (HAP1)8. A library of mutagenized cells, carrying knockouts in virtually all non-essential genes, was infected with an AAV2 vector that expresses red fluorescent protein (RFP) (Extended Data Fig. 2a). Mutant cells refractory to AAV2 infection were isolated through iterative cycles of fluorescence-activated cell sorting (Extended Data Fig. 2b). Cellular entry of adeno-associated viruses (AAV) is poorly understood, despite the prominent use of AAV vectors in gene therapy for several monogenic diseases. Using an unbiased, haploid genetic screen, we identified critical players in AAV serotype 2 (AAV2) entry including members of distinct protein complexes involved in retrograde trafficking as well as genes involved in the biosynthesis of the AAV2 attachment factor, heparan sulphate. We focused on the single most significantly enriched gene of the screen, an uncharacterized type-I transmembrane protein. Based on the evidence below we renamed this gene AAV receptor (AAVR). We discovered AAVR as capable of rapidly endocytosing from the plasma membrane and trafficking to the trans-Golgi network, taking a similar path as AAV particles utilize. Genetic ablation of *AAVR* using CRISPR/Cas9 technology demonstrated a robust resistance to AAV2 infection in a wide range of mammalian cell types, which could be reversed upon *AAVR* complementation. This confirmed the essentiality of AAVR in AAV2 infection. Further investigation revealed that AAVR was also required for the infections of all tested human and simian-derived AAV serotypes including AAV1, 3B, 5, 6, 8 and 9. Deeper characterization of AAVR showed it to contain Ig-like domains, which are commonly found in many virus receptors including those for poliovirus and measles. We observed that these domains are capable of binding to AAV2 particles, and anti-AAVR antibodies efficiently block AAV2 infection. Moreover, the importance of AAVR for AAV infection *in vivo* was demonstrated by the strong resistance of AAVR−/− mice to AAV9 infection, recapitulating what we showed *in vitro*. Collectively, the data indicates that AAVR is a universal receptor involved in AAV infection. This has significant implications for the improvement of future AAV vector design.

## Abstract

Developing vehicles that efficiently deliver genes throughout the human central nervous system (CNS) will broaden the range of treatable genetic diseases. We engineered an adeno-associated virus (AAV) capsid, BI-hTFR1, that binds human transferrin receptor (TfR1), a protein expressed on the blood-brain barrier. We chose TfR1 as a target because of its high expression on the human BBB; its ability to mediate constitutive, ligand-independent receptor-mediated transcytosis (RMT) across the CNS vasculature (8– 12); and its track record as a target to increase the delivery of biologics into the CNS of mice (13– 15), nonhuman primates (NHPs) (16– 18), and humans as investigational therapies (19– 22) and as an approved antibody-based therapeutic for Mucopolysaccharidosis type II (23). The top-performing capsid, AAV-BI-hTFR1, exhibited more efficient gene delivery to human brain endothelial cells and improved active transport across a human vascular monolayer. When systemically administered to adult TFRC knock-in (KI) mice carrying a chimeric Tfrc gene with a humanized extracellular domain, BI-hTFR1 transduced the majority of neurons and astrocytes across multiple brain regions. The enhanced tropism was entirely dependent on an interaction with the humanized TfR1, as we observed no enhancement in wild type (WT) mice. The tropism was also selectively enhanced in the CNS, consistent with the high level of expression of TFRC on the CNS vasculature relative to the vasculature in other organs (12).

To explore its ability to deliver a therapeutically relevant cargo, we intravenously injected TFRC KI mice with BI-hTFR1 or AAV9 packaging the human Glucosylceramidase Beta 1 (GBA1) gene. Systemic delivery of BI-hTFR1: GBA1 in adult TFRC KI mice resulted in increased expression throughout the brain and elevated glucocerebrosidase (GCase) activity in the brain and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which were not observed with AAV9. S7A) (45). Under the same imaging conditions, GBA-HA was not detected in the brains of the mice injected with the high dose of AAV9. This suggests that a 20-fold lower dose of BI-hTFR1 led to greater GBA levels in disease-relevant brain regions compared to AAV9.

...

In this study, we leveraged a well established mechanism—engagement of the apical domain of human TfR1—to shuttle an engineered AAV capsid, BI-hTFR1, across the BBB. Protein shuttles designed to bind human TfR1 to facilitate RMT are now in the clinic and are showing evidence of CNS entry (NCT04023994) and efficacy (46). The TfR1 apical domain is also a receptor target of natural viruses (47– 51), indicating that this protein can be exploited for viral entry. Importantly, we demonstrated that BI-hTFR1 binds human TfR1 and pre-formed TfR1-Tf complexes with comparable kinetics and does not compete with holo-Tf for TfR1 binding. The ability to bind TfR1 in the presence of its natural ligand is critical because AAVs cannot be administered at doses capable of competing with Tf for TfR1 binding. The use of this validated transport mechanism bolsters our confidence that BI-hTFR1 can perform well as a CNS-targeting human gene therapy vehicle.

...

We engineered BI-hTFR1 to bind TfR1 by inserting a novel 7-mer TfR1 recognition sequence directly within surface loop VIII of the capsid. Because our approach did not require the introduction or conjugation of bulky protein domains as a means to retarget the AAV (52– 58), we do not anticipate additional complexities in the manufacturing of BI-hTFR1 compared to AAV9, one of the top producing natural AAVs. Indeed, we consistently produced and purified BI-hTFR1 with final yields comparable to those of AAV9, and determined that BI-hTFR1 can be purified with affinity resins commonly used in AAV manufacturing (fig. S8)

...

As compared to natural AAV capsids such as AAV9 and AAV2 that are used in approved gene therapies, BI-hTFR1 demonstrated the remarkable ability to be actively transported across a human brain endothelial cell layer and to cross the BBB and transduce cells throughout the brains and spinal cords of TFRC KI mice after intravenous delivery. BI-hTFR1 exhibited a broad CNS tropism enhancement similar to those observed with engineered mouse BBB-crossing capsids, e.g., AAV-PHP.B, BI28, AAVF, and 9P31 that bind to mouse GPI-anchored proteins LY6A, LY6C1, or Car4 (25, 59, 60). By engaging highly abundant CNS endothelial cell surface proteins as new receptors, these capsids are able to efficiently cross the BBB and gain access to parenchymal cells.

...

Collectively, our results demonstrate that BI-hTFR1 can leverage the RMT activity of human TfR1 to cross the BBB and deliver genes widely and efficiently to neurons and glia throughout the CNS. These qualities provide strong support for the further exploration of BI-hTFR1 as a broadly applicable vehicle for human CNS gene therapies.

Title: New Gene Delivery Method Paves the Way for Advanced Brain Therapies - National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH)
URL: https://www.nimh.nih.gov/news/science-updates/2024/new-gene-delivery-method-paves-the-way-for-advanced-brain-therapies
Published: 2024-08-15T00:00:00.000Z
Author: N/A
Highlights:
A new study, funded by the National Institute of Mental Health and the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke, describes a promising way to carry genetic material into the brain to reach cellular targets. The researchers developed a delivery vehicle that can effectively transport genes across the blood-brain barrier by latching onto a human protein and distributing its genetic cargo to cells in the brain. Although the researchers have not yet tested the approach in people, this study brings us closer to making many life-saving treatments a reality.

...

The researchers started by looking for an AAV with a high chance of reaching the human brain. In previous work, Deverman’s lab had already developed an efficient way of engineering new AAVs by looking for ones that bind to specific proteins on the surface of target cells or organs.

They used that method to create and screen a library of different AAVs to see if any would bind to a protein called human transferrin receptor (TfR1), which brings iron into the brain. TfR1 is highly expressed on the human blood-brain barrier and has been shown to shuttle large molecules across that barrier to reach the brain in studies with humans.

This step narrowed down the candidate AAVs to one, named BI-hTFR1, that could attach itself to the TfR1 protein. With a promising AAV identified, the researchers next tested the AAV in human cells and in mice modified to express the human form of the TfR1 protein. They also examined whether the new AAV could transport genetic material into the brain, comparing it with one of the few currently existing AAVs able to deliver genes to the human central nervous system.

...

First, the researchers found that the TfR1-bound AAV successfully crossed the blood-brain barrier in the human cell model. Moreover, in a head-to-head comparison with the existing AAV used in nervous system gene therapies, significantly more of the new AAV actively traveled across the brain cell barrier.

This finding was further supported when the researchers injected the AAV into the bloodstream of mice expressing the human form of TfR1. Results showed that the new AAV successfully entered the brain and spinal cord of the mice and did so at much higher levels than the existing AAV, showing 6–12 times greater amounts across the brain. Importantly, this effect was not found for other organs, demonstrating the new AAV’s enhanced entry into the central nervous system. The AAV also affected brain cells with critical functions, reaching up to 92% of astrocytes and 71% of neurons , which play important roles in how cells develop and communicate.

Last, the researchers examined the AAV’s ability to deliver the human gene GBA1 into the mouse brain. Mutations in the GBA1 gene are linked to several neurodegenerative disorders, including Gaucher disease and Parkinson’s disease. The new AAV delivered the GBA1 gene throughout the brain. Once again, the results emphasized the enhanced effectiveness of the new AAV, which delivered 30 times more copies of GBA1 compared to the existing AAV. Together, the results showed that the AAV can effectively enter the brain at a large scale and carry with it healthy copies of genetic material.

...

These findings confirm that AAVs can be targeted to specific proteins to create powerful, minimally invasive gene delivery vehicles. The researchers in this study engineered an AAV that, by directly binding to a human receptor protein, crossed the blood-brain barrier to reach critical cells and deliver a disease-relevant gene throughout the brain.

Importantly, the new AAV was more effective and efficient than the main AAV currently used for nervous system gene therapies. Another critical advantage was its human-specific binding. Because the AAV binds to a well-studied human protein found at the blood-brain barrier, the researchers think it has strong potential to work for human gene therapies. Using mice that express the human form of the Tfr1 receptor also provides strong evidence that this therapy could show success in people.

Although exciting, the results require further testing in human studies. The researchers will also need to address common challenges that face any AAV gene therapy, including limits on the size of the gene it can deliver, potential off-target impacts on other genes or gene pathways, and the risk of an overactive immune system response. Despite these hurdles, with further testing and development, the gene delivery method could open up new therapeutic avenues and revolutionize treatment for a range of neurological and mental disorders.
